analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 an hour and ends the tipped, youth, and disabled-worker subminimum wages.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act of 2025, backed by 34 of 45 Senate Democrats plus its independent sponsor, was referred to the Senate labor committee in April 2025 and has had no markup or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps over five years, from today's $7.25 an hour to $9.50 right away, then $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and finally $17. After that, the wage would automatically rise with the growth in the median worker's pay. It would also phase out the lower 'subminimum' wages now allowed for tipped workers, teenagers under 20 in their first 90 days, and some workers with disabilities, until everyone is covered by the same wage floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 20 million or more low-wage workers would see raises, with the biggest gains for workers in states with no minimum wage above $7.25, for tipped restaurant workers whose cash wage would climb to $17, and for workers with disabilities now paid under special certificates. Tipped employees would also gain the explicit legal right to keep all their tips.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $9.50 an hour shortly after enactment, then in annual steps to $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and $17, after which it rises automatically with median wage growth so it never stagnates again [S2].

Eliminates the separate lower minimum wage for tipped employees, raising their guaranteed cash wage from $2.13 to $17 over about six years, and gives employees the explicit right to retain their tips [S2].

Phases out the $4.25 training wage for newly hired workers under 20 and ends the authority to pay workers with disabilities less than the full minimum wage, while directing the Labor Department to help employers transition to competitive employment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay less than the new minimums — restaurants and other food service, hospitality, retail, and providers of services to people with disabilities — would bear higher labor costs, which could be passed to consumers through higher prices or absorbed through lower profits and, in some cases, fewer jobs or hours. Small businesses with thin margins would face the steepest adjustment.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face a federal wage floor roughly 134% higher within five years, and the steepest burden falls on labor-intensive businesses like restaurants, where the separate tipped wage is eliminated entirely rather than left to state choice [S2].

Critics of large minimum wage increases argue that employers respond by cutting hours, reducing staff, automating tasks, or raising prices, and that the heaviest losses fall on exactly the entry-level workers the bill aims to help; the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has previously estimated that a $15 federal minimum would cost some jobs while raising pay for far more workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A large majority of affected workers would get substantial raises, and indexing to median wages would prevent the floor from eroding again. The genuine costs are concentrated on low-margin employers and, in the estimates of most economists who study the question, some reduction in employment among the least-experienced workers. The phased schedule and small-business transition assistance for disability providers soften but do not eliminate that trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and in the months since it has not received a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on April 8, 2025, with 33 Democratic senators joining as original cosponsors [S1][S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on April 8, 2025 [S4].
As of the latest action record, the committee has taken no further action: no markup, no hearing on the bill, and no floor vote have been scheduled [S4].
Cosponsorship stands at 34 of 45 Senate Democrats, and no Senate Republican has cosponsored [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the current $7.25 federal minimum, and the tipped-restaurant sector, are better off because the bill has gone nowhere; workers earning near the federal minimum keep waiting for a raise.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers, at least for now

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors are independents or Democrats — 34 of 45 Senate Democrats plus the sponsor — and no Republican has signed on, while Republicans hold the Senate majority and chair the committee where the bill sits.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the $2.13 tipped minimum wage and requires a full $17 hourly wage, sharply raising labor costs for an industry that employs millions at low pay. Its interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the wage gains tipped workers would receive.

industries.industry: Hospitality, retail, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Employers with large numbers of workers paid between $7.25 and $17 would face steep, phased payroll increases, some of which would be passed on in prices or offset through staffing cuts. Their cost is the workers' gain.

industries.industry: Providers of services to people with disabilities using subminimum-wage certificates
industries.note: The bill raises the minimum for 14(c) certificate holders to the full wage within five years and bans new certificates, while offering federal transition assistance. These employers' business model depends on paying less than the minimum wage, which the bill ends.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, chairing the HELP Committee, and offering no cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to receive a markup or floor vote this Congress. Absent a change in Senate control or a major political shift, the most likely path is that it dies in committee at the end of the session, the fate of most previous federal minimum wage bills, though states continue to raise their own minimums.
